newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: APEC leaders gather for summit to forge free trade.
newsitem.headline: APEC leaders gather for summit to forge free trade.

text.p: Asia-Pacific leaders wielding half the world's economic might met on Monday to draw up an action plan for the biggest free trade and investment zone on earth.

U.S. President Bill Clinton was preparing a final push for adoption of a U.S. plan to free trade in information technology, building blocks of the 21st century, at the Asia-Pacific Econonomic Cooperation summit in Subic Bay.

According to an early draft of a declaration, the leaders called on the World Trade Organisation (WTO) to ink an agreement eliminating substantial tariffs on computers, memory chips and telecommunications equipment.
But advance copies of the draft leaked to Philippine media said it "recognised the need for flexibility".

Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin, fresh from their breakthrough Sunday announcement of summit talks in each other's capital, and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto were among leaders who flew into Subic Bay from Manila.
Subic was once a major U.S. naval base and is now a development zone that symbolises the Philippines dreams of becoming a new Asian tiger.

Meeting in a former U.S. military officer's club surrounded by jungle overlooking a deep bay where America's Pacific battle fleets used to shelter, the leaders were to adopt a detailed plan of action they hope will set the region on a settled course for peaceful development for the next century.
Not all the leaders agreed exactly on how to do it. The United States wants to fling all markets open in a trade free-for-all.
Some of the heads of developing Asian countries, such as Malaysia's Mahathir Mohamed, want to move ahead more gingerly and are chafing at the pressure.

APEC has pledged to abolish all obstacles to trade in developed countries by 2010 and in developing nations by 2020 to create a borderless economy embracing two billion people with 40 percent of global trade and more than half of economic output.
A four-page draft of the declaration called for "freer and non-discriminatory trade in goods and services".
"We call on WTO members to build on the process of progressive liberalisation and enhanced transparency we have initiated at APEC," it said.
"We are determined that our efforts at APEC should serve as a catalyst to the liberalisation of the multilateral trading system."
U.S. officials see APEC's support of their Information Technology agreement as a test of its resolve to become a real power in global trade rather than a talking shop.

Thousands of leftwing demonstrators who streamed out of the capital in a caravan of jeepneys -- minibus copies of U.S. World War Two jeeps -- abandoned their plans to roll into the heavily-guarded summit site.
Protest leaders said they were putting the brakes on the cavalcade because it would be "suicidal" in the face of resistance by riot police.
More than 7,000 protesters set off for Subic Bay, 80 km (50 miles) to the north of Manila, but numerous police roadblocks and rain delayed their progress.

An informal dinner of APEC leaders on Sunday gave Clinton an opportunity to lobby on information technology ahead of the WTO's first ministerial meeting in Singapore next month. Half a billion dollars a year of trade is at stake, most of it generated in Asia Pacific nations led by the United States.
At the summit centre, leaders will discuss in formal and informal sessions how to realise their aim of barrier-free trade.

Against a backdrop of the sweeping bay, the leaders of nations from China to Papua New Guinea and Chile strode across manucured lawns into the summit hall dressed in traditional bleached white Philippine barong shirts.
They were greeted by Philippine President Fidel Ramos, looking relaxed and casual and clutching a cigar.
The controversial question of China's membership of the WTO was likely to come up.

As well as freeing trade and investment flows, APEC aims to promote technical cooperation in areas like transort, energy, telecommunications and infrastructure development. It also intends to make life easier for businessmen by streamlining regulations on customs, standards and testing.
